backups.name: West Face / South Summit (Standard)
backups.fa: Unknown — the peak's 1930 first ascent (Forest Farr, Art Winder, Laurence Byington) was via the south/east face, not this line
gear: two ropes, or a 60m lead rope plus a tag line (the Rappel Chimney rappel is rigged two-strand)
cams (helpful for parallel-sided cracks on P1-P2)
glacier kit (axe, crampons or microspikes late-season)
hazards: rockfall
crevasses on the approach glacier
exposed summit pitch
long approach
backups.overview: Chimney Rock is one of the most striking and sought-after technical summits of the Alpine Lakes high country, a twin-towered spire rising above the Lemah and Summit Chief peaks. The standard line gains the higher south summit by a committing glacier approach and several pitches of moderate rock high above remote lake basins.
backups.beta: From the upper Chimney Glacier, ascend the prominent gully between the main summit and south peak. Follow Class 3-4 scrambling on debris and snow, traversing ledges through the couloir. Continue with Class 4-5 rock climbing on slabs and chimneys to gain the summit. The route involves both snow and rock sections requiring helmets and protection.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time of 1:00-2:00 PM on summit day. If summit is not reached by this time, descent must begin immediately to ensure arrival at base camp before full darkness. Weather deterioration, technical difficulty, or team member struggle are valid turnaround triggers regardless of proximity to summit.
backups.rappels: 2 rappels: a short single-strand rap off the summit, then a two-strand rap down the Rappel Chimney - a second rope or tag line is required
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
backups.comms: Cell phone coverage is limited to nonexistent above Pete Lake. Verizon may have weak signal at lower elevations of approach. Satellite communication device (personal locator beacon, Garmin inReach, or satellite messengers) highly recommended for emergency contact.
backups.descent: Rappel and downclimb the ascent route

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency Pass honored in the lot; fill out the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Reached on FR-4616 off Cooper Lake Road, past Cooper Lake.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and established shoreline campsites on the north side; the last easy water before the PCT junction.
waypoints.directions: Roughly four miles of easy, nearly flat forest trail. The tread is in good shape and gets dusty by midsummer, and it is walked fast — none of the day's real work is here.

waypoints.name: PCT Junction near Lemah Meadows
waypoints.note: Pete Lake Trail meets the PCT here; turn north toward Lemah Meadows rather than continuing to Spectacle Lake.
waypoints.directions: Carry on past the lake on the Pete Lake Trail to where it meets the PCT — a short, gentle stretch. Fill up before leaving the lake; above here water means Chimney Creek or melted snow.

waypoints.name: Climber's trail, east side of Chimney Creek
waypoints.note: A climber's path, marked with orange flagging in places, follows the east bank of Chimney Creek up toward Sunrise Knob, staying above the avalanche debris used by the East Face approach.
waypoints.directions: Head north on the PCT about a mile to where it crosses the Chimney Creek avalanche path, and leave the trail there. A logjam gives the creek crossing, and the climber's path starts faint on the far side, running about twenty yards inside the forest alongside the avalanche slope before it firms up. Losing the start puts you in the brush of the avalanche path itself, which is what the flagging is there to prevent.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Knob
waypoints.note: Shared basecamp for both Chimney Rock routes, on a knob just below the moraine overlooking the falls.
waypoints.directions: Steep, brushy climbing up the east bank, crossing several ravines, to the rock buttress at the top. Budget four to five hours from the car to here — the mileage is modest but nearly all the gain and all the route-finding sit in this last stretch.

waypoints.name: West-side glacier / moat crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the small glacier on the west side of the peak below the face; the moat widens through late season and can force a detour by August.
waypoints.directions: Climb the moraine above camp to the glacier; a wet, grubby gully through the rock band is the usual way onto the ice. Rope up and cross the lower glacier bearing toward the toe of the south peak rather than the main-summit gully the East Face uses. Little is known about this connection, so budget route-finding time and be ready to improvise around the moat at the base of the face.

waypoints.name: Notch between the summits
waypoints.note: Roughly three pitches (~600 vertical ft) of wet, slippery ledges and cracks gain this notch between the central and south summits; also used as a rappel/downclimb station on descent.
waypoints.directions: Off the glacier, the line starts in left-slanting grooves and cracks about thirty to forty feet climber's-right of the obvious Rappel Chimney. Higher up it passes through a chimney that is not visible from the base and which climbs and protects easily. Everything on this aspect stays wet, so the short fourth-class steps feel harder than their grade.

waypoints.name: Chimney Rock, South Summit
waypoints.note: South Summit, about 400 vertical feet above the notch; descend by downclimbing/rappelling back to the notch and the northwest-shoulder rappel station.
waypoints.directions: The ground eases off toward the top, finishing at the large, noticeably rocking block that doubles as the top anchor for the descent. This is Chimney Rock's south summit, not the main summit that the East Face route climbs. Coming down reverses the line: a short rappel off the north side back to the northwest shoulder, then a full double-rope rappel down the Rappel Chimney, and downclimbing from there to the glacier.

sectionBreakdown.note: Same approach as the East Face: Pete Lake trailhead to Pete Lake, join the PCT, then a climber's path up steep, brushy terrain to a bivy camp around 4,650-4,800 ft at the southern …
Cross the glacier toe to the base of the West Face, then climb 3 pitches — an awkward crack/groove pitch, a ladder-like chimney, and a final pitch of large tumbled blocks that's mo…
Break camp and hike back down to Pete Lake and the trailhead.

backups.detailed_rack: Bring a comprehensive trad rack including stoppers (even and odd sizes), full set of single cams from BD #0 to #3 with emphasis on larger 1-2 inch sizes for parallel-sided cracks, and doubles of common sizes. Include slings (multiple lengths), quickdraws (8-10), and runners for expedient protection placement on loose terrain.
pro_tips: Cross the glacier early when firm
Build in time for the long approach and multiple rappels
Pitch 1's leftward-angling groove/crack system is awkward to protect — rack accordingly.
backups.pro_needs: A standard rack of nuts/stoppers plus cams for the parallel-sided cracks on the lower two pitches; a single 50m rope covers the route and the rappels from the northwest-shoulder station.
backups.approach: This route shares the same trailhead-to-basin approach as the East Face: from the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616, hike the Pete Lake Trail #1323 (~4 easy miles to Pete Lake, then ~2 more miles) to the Pacific Crest Trail junction, head north on the PCT about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche-path crossing, then leave the PCT and follow the climber's path (flagged/cairned, fords Chimney Creek and crosses several brushy ravines) up through Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft, ~4-5 hrs from the trailhead) to the moraine and the bivy basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier (~5,400 ft) — see the East Face route's approach text for full turn-by-turn detail on this shared stretch, and treat it as a 2-3 day car-to-car trip. Pitch 1 reportedly starts in grooves and cracks roughly 30-40 feet climber's-right of the obvious 'Rappel Chimney' feature on the west face, reached via a short glacier crossing and scramble from the basin; this specific glacier-to-base connection is less well known than the East Face line, so budget extra route-finding time and be ready to improvise around the moat at the base of the face, which gets worse later in the season. Water and camping options match the East Face approach: Pete Lake, the low Chimney Creek crossings, or melted glacier snow above the moraine.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the West Face rather than continuing along the ridge. From the true summit, make a short ~40-foot single-strand rappel down the north side to regain the northwest shoulder and the large, distinctively rocking summit block, which serves as the anchor/belay at the top of the route's 2nd pitch. From the shoulder, make a full double-rope (two-strand) rappel down the aptly named 'Rappel Chimney' on a fixed/bolted anchor — which gets you down far enough that the remaining short section to the glacier is straightforward downclimbing rather than a third rappel. Because the second rappel is rigged double-strand, bring a full second rope long enough to comfortably reach the lower stance (it doesn't need to be full climbing-diameter — many parties pair a thin tag line with the lead rope to save weight). Total rappels: 2 (short single-strand rap off the summit, then the longer double-rope Rappel Chimney rap). Carry a few feet of extra webbing/cord and a couple of rap rings, especially in early season, in case the fixed anchor material is worn, buried in snow, or needs backing up. From the base of the rappels, reverse the glacier crossing and the moraine/climber's path back to Sunrise Knob and the Pete Lake Trail.
backups.bail: From high camp or glacier base, descend back down Pete Lake trail to trailhead. If above the main rock buttress before full commitment to climbing, retreat down gully and across glacier toward base camp. If committed to rock sections, retreat becomes fixed-anchor-dependent; carry emergency bivy gear. Poor weather on summit day warrants turnaround decision by 1:00 PM to ensure safe descent before darkness.

pitch_detail.notes: Start in grooves and cracks roughly 30-40 ft climber's-right of the 'Rappel Chimney' feature; the route's technical crux, per the route's Class 5.6 rating.
Continue up the west face on moderate terrain toward the northwest shoulder.
Easier climbing to the large, distinctively rocking summit block, which also serves as the top anchor for the descent.

itinerary.cal: Same season window as the East Face (July-September); the West Face stays drier since it avoids the East Face moat/bergschrund crossing, but snow patches on the glacier approach can persist into midsummer.

days.note: Same approach as the East Face: Pete Lake trailhead to Pete Lake, join the PCT, then a climber's path up steep, brushy terrain to a bivy camp around 4,650-4,800 ft at the southern toe of the Chimney Glacier.

days.note: Cross the glacier toe to the base of the West Face, then climb 3 pitches — an awkward crack/groove pitch, a ladder-like chimney, and a final pitch of large tumbled blocks that's mostly scrambling to the summit. Descend with a short rap to the northwest shoulder followed by a longer double-rope rappel down the 'Rappel Chimney', downclimbing the rest to the glacier.

crowds.peakTraffic: If any traffic occurs it clusters on August weekends in stable weather; solo/rare encounters with other parties are the norm, not the exception.
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - Chimney Rock overall is anecdotally described (via summit register mentions) as seeing roughly one ascent party per year across all its routes; the West Face/South Summit line sees fewer parties than the more commonly climbed East Face, likely only a handful of parties in a good season.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong, sustained hiking fitness for a long wilderness approach (Pete Lake Trail plus off-trail climber's path and glacier travel) with significant elevation gain in a single push or over an overnight backpack.
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Moderate-heavy: overnight/bivy gear (many parties camp near Pete Lake or higher to break up the long approach), a rock rack, glacier kit (rope, harness, crevasse-rescue hardware), and helmet for rockfall.

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long approach: roughly 4-6 miles one-way on the Pete Lake Trail to Pete Lake (~2,980 ft) followed by an off-trail climber's path and lower Chimney Glacier crossing to the base of the West Face; exact hour count not confirmed in sources, but the approach alone is commonly broken into an overnight backpack rather than done car-to-car in one push.
requiredSkills: Basic glacier travel and crevasse rescue (roped crossing of the Chimney Glacier on approach)
Route-finding on an unmarked climber's path and broken alpine terrain
Rockfall awareness/management in the chimney systems
Self-sufficiency for a long, remote day with no reliable outside help nearby
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine climber comfortable leading loose, sometimes wet Class 5.6 rock in a remote setting, with prior glacier-travel and self-rescue experience; not a beginner objective given the long approach, glacier crossing, and rockfall-prone chimneys already noted in the route's hazards.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-to-late August is the sweet spot within  of August.

July.reason: Route becomes viable late in the month as per the season window, but early-to-mid July can still have lingering snow on approach ledges and in the chimneys.

June.reason: Snow-covered with the approach glacier well filled and elevated avalanche risk; well before the season starts.

August.reason: Matches the existing best-season; rock is driest and the glacier crossing firms up overnight.

September.reason: Still within the season, but existing beta flags a shortening window with the bergschrund/crevasses opening up late season and less settled weather.

weather.typical: Wet maritime climate near the crest; clearest and driest mid-to-late summer with the glacier firming overnight in the prime August window.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorm buildup is plausible in August given the Cascade crest location; precipitation frequency increases moving into September as the season's short fall window closes.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence: sustained rockfall exposure in the chimneys, an exposed summit pitch with limited protection, and a long, glaciated, remote approach that magnifies the seriousness of any injury, storm, or rockfall incident.

avalanche.zone: Approximate Stevens Pass / East Slopes Central NWAC zone boundary area (Alpine Lakes crest near Cooper Lake) - no NWAC zone precisely covers this peak, and the route is not normally climbed during avalanche season.

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Real hazard, not N/A: the route crosses the lower Chimney Glacier on approach to the West Face, with crevasses on the approach glacier and open crevasses late season - rope travel and basic crevasse-rescue capability are warranted, especially in September.

backups.rope_note: Documented Chimney Rock routes are predominantly on the East Face (3 pitches: chimney, slab, chimney, low-5th). The West Face/South Summit line has limited independent documentation — the rack here is sized by comparison with the East Face standard route, as the closest analog.

Full double-rope rappel down the Rappel Chimney; gets low enough that the remaining descent to the glacier is a downclimb rather than a third rappel.

backups.rappel_count_note: Two rappels. This line is sparsely documented, and no fixed hardware at the Rappel Chimney anchor is confirmed for this peak — inspect whatever is there and carry webbing, cord and rings to back it up or replace it, especially in early season when the anchor may be worn or buried.

approach_variants.name: Chimney Glacier to the west face
approach_variants.notes: Shares the whole trailhead-to-basin stretch with the East Face line: the Pete Lake Trail to the lake, on to the Pacific Crest Trail, north about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche path, then a flagged climbers' path on the east bank of Chimney Creek up through steep brush and several ravines to Sunrise Knob at about 4,650 ft and the bivy basin at the toe of the glacier. Budget four to five hours car to knob and treat the whole outing as two or three days. Above camp, climb the moraine and take the wet, grubby gully through the rock band onto the ice, then rope up and cross the lower glacier bearing toward the toe of the south peak rather than the main-summit gully.
hazards: Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier
A moat at the base of the face that widens badly through late season
Rock that stays wet on this aspect, so short fourth-class steps feel harder than their grade
Rockfall out of the gullies above the glacier
Long, remote approach with no quick retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding: The reference feature is the Rappel Chimney — the obvious clean cleft splitting the west face, and the line you will come back down. Pitch one starts in left-slanting grooves and cracks roughly thirty to forty feet climber's-RIGHT of it. Getting that side wrong matters: starting in the chimney itself puts you on the descent line rather than the route. The other trap is that the correct start looks blank and unpromising from the ground, because the chimney that makes the second pitch straightforward is not visible from the base at all — it climbs and protects like a ladder once you are in it. Aim the glacier crossing at the toe of the SOUTH peak; the gully between the main summit and the south peak is the East Face line's ground, and drifting into it takes you onto a different climb. Expect to improvise around the moat at the foot of the face, which gets worse the later in the season you come, and expect the connection from ice to rock to take longer than the neighbouring line, so budget route-finding time rather than assuming you will step straight onto the first pitch.

climbing_route.label: Lower Chimney Glacier to the toe of the south peak
climbing_route.notes: From the bivy basin, rope up and cross the lower Chimney Glacier, working toward the toe of the south peak rather than the main-summit gully used by the East Face. Be ready to improvise around the moat at the base of the face, which gets worse later in the season.

climbing_route.label: Pitch 1 — grooves and cracks right of the Rappel Chimney
climbing_route.notes: Pitch 1 reportedly starts in grooves and cracks roughly 30-40 feet climber's-right of the obvious 'Rappel Chimney' feature on the west face, reached via a short glacier crossing and scramble from the basin. This glacier-to-base connection is less well known than the East Face line, so budget extra route-finding time.

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
bivy.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
bivy.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

backups.name: North Norwegian Buttress
backups.fa: Pete Doorish, solo, 1980s (aid). First free ascent: Nathan Hadley with Luke Stefurak, Michal Rynkiewicz, and Stamati Anagnostou, August 2023 ('Bluebell', 5.13-)
gear: bolted anchors on the newer lines (Jötnar, Bluebell) — inspect fixed gear before fully weighting
hazards: steep committing buttress
loose and vegetated rock
notoriously difficult approach
route-finding
backups.overview: The North Norwegian Buttress is a striking, roughly 2,000-foot buttress on Mount Index's northwest aspect, plainly visible from busy US 2 above Lake Serene, separated from the smaller South Norwegian Buttress by a deep cleft between the Main and Middle summits. Despite its prominence it saw little traffic for decades — Pete Doorish's 1980s solo aid line was the only route until the Voodoo Project (2002) and Jötnar (2020, VI 5.9 A3+, 16 pitches) added further aid lines. Nathan Hadley's Bluebell (first freed August 2023; 21 pitches, 5.13-, roughly a third overhanging, entirely bolt-protected) is the first free route up the buttress and one of the hardest big walls established in the Cascades.
backups.beta: The North Norwegian Buttress is one of the larger walls in the Lower 48, plainly visible from Highway 2. Multiple big-wall routes exist on this face, ranging from Grade VI 5.9 A3+ (Jötnar) to free climbing lines (Bluebell, 5.13-). The buttress is separated from the South Norwegian Buttress by a deep cleft between the Main and Middle Peaks. Most parties approach via Lake Serene.
backups.turnaround: Set a conservative turnaround; retreat is complex on this committing face.
backups.rappels: Single 70m rope; every belay is bolted and rap-equipped, with dedicated rap-line anchors that let parties skip some belays for a faster single-rope descent, especially through the Headwall.
backups.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: No cell service at elevation. Satellite communicator (InReach, Spot) strongly recommended for multi-day wall climb.
backups.descent: Descent is typically by rappelling the route itself, using a single uncut 70m rope on the bolted lines (per the Bluebell first free ascent); older aid lines share similar rappel anchors down the same buttress rather than a walk-off via the standard Mount Index descent.
obj_haz: Rockfall off North Index and the gully between the buttress and Middle Index
Loose, chossy wide cracks on the aid lines
Seasonal waterfall/water flow low on the route

backups.pro_needs: Aid rack up to A3+ for Jötnar, the representative modern aid line; the original 1980s Doorish solo line was easier, roughly A2. Newer lines (Jötnar, Bluebell) are largely bolt-protected.

backups.approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead (~600 ft) off Mount Index Road, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail — roughly 3.6-4.1 miles (accounts vary slightly) and about 2,000 ft of gain, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur around mile 1.6 and switchbacking up to Lake Serene (~2,600 ft). At the lake, leave the maintained trail for the unofficial climbers' path that traverses talus and large boulders around the west side of the lake; in early summer this crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow/ice at the lake's edge. Continue up talus beneath the imposing north/east face of North Index toward the cirque below the Norwegian Buttresses, then work up through the brushy base of the wall — steepening mossy slabs and brush that some parties rope up for before reaching clean rock on the buttress proper. Reliable water is available at Lake Serene and its outlet creek, but not higher on the talus approach, so fill up at the lake. Plan roughly 2-3 hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, more with a loaded pack for a multi-day ascent.
backups.descent_text: The North Norwegian Buttress is descended by rappelling the route itself, not via a walk-off. On the two documented lines — Jötnar (VI 5.9 A3+, 16 pitches) and its free variant Bluebell (5.13-, 21 pitches) — nearly every belay is bolted (on Jötnar, all anchors are bolted except one gear belay near pitch 15), and Bluebell's full 2,000 ft can reportedly be descended on a single, uncut 70m rope rappelling single-strand station to station. That works out to roughly 9-10 long single-strand rappels for the full wall, though a party descending pitch-by-pitch off every bolted ascent anchor could instead make closer to 15-16 shorter rappels — the actual count depends on how many stations you link together with the longer rope. Expect some overhanging pitches where you'll need to swing or place directional protection to reach the next station cleanly, and expect the descent to take nearly as long as the climb. Retrieve any fixed lines left during the ascent as you go (established leave-no-trace practice on this route), then reverse the talus traverse around Lake Serene to the maintained trail.
backups.bail: Retreat is involved on the steep buttress; commit only with experience and good conditions.

approach_variants.notes: Maintained trail to Lake Serene past the Bridal Veil Falls spur, then the unofficial climbers' path around the right-hand (west) shore over talus and large boulders, down granite slabs, and up the talus fan to the wall. Fill water at the lake — there is none above it. In early summer the lakeside traverse crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow at the water's edge. Two to three hours from the car with a light pack, appreciably more with a loaded haul bag for a multi-day ascent.
hazards: Large natural rockfall off North Index and out of the cleft beside Middle Index
Avalanche debris and lingering snow at the lake edge in early summer
Steepening mossy slabs and brush at the base that parties rope up for
Loose and vegetated rock low on the wall
No walk-off — every retreat from the buttress is by rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identify the wall before committing to any line on it. The North Norwegian Buttress is the roughly 2,000-foot face on Mount Index's northwest side rising directly above the head of the lake, and it is separated from the smaller South Norwegian Buttress by a deep cleft running up between the Main and Middle summits. That cleft is the boundary between the two buttresses and it is also the chute that funnels stonefall onto the approach, so work up the talus fan to the toe rather than traversing in high across the base. The bottom of the buttress is not the bottom of the climbing: below the clean granite lies a band of steepening mossy slab and brush, and the change from vegetated slab to continuous rock is where the pitches actually begin. Across the face the routes are located by counting off the Doorish line, the original aid line up the buttress, so find that first and work from it. Rack up low, near the lake, and keep your time directly beneath the wall short.

bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, on slab and talus. That spot sits close to the edge of the quarter-mile no-camping ring, probably just outside it but not by a comfortable margin, so sleep as high and as far from the shore as the ground allows and be ready to move if asked. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
bivy.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

bivy.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
bivy.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
bivy.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
bivy.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Red Pass, then the climbers' path up to the saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT trailhead at exit 52, hike the PCT north about two miles to the Commonwealth Creek / Red Mountain Trail #1033 junction. Follow that trail, crossing Commonwealth Creek, roughly 1.7 miles further, passing Red Mountain on your right and Red Pond on your left, to the Red Mountain Saddle — Red Pass — at about 5,320 ft. The old PCT dropped from here toward Goldmyer Hot Springs.

From the saddle, follow a winding climbers' path up to the base of the route. Allow about two hours for the approach from the trailhead, more if there is snow.

This is a short technical add-on for parties already scrambling in the Red Pass and Commonwealth Basin area, not a day out on its own.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THREE OVERSIZED BOLTS ARE THE PROOF, AND THEY ARE THE REASON THIS ROUTE IS FINDABLE AT ALL. The pitch carries THREE fixed bolts, described by everyone who has climbed it as monstrous — large enough that they make the route-finding non-adventurous. If you are on a 30 m pitch of broken rock with three big bolts in it, you are on this route. If you cannot see a bolt, you are on the ridge somewhere else.

WHAT THE PITCH IS: a very short 30 m lead, broken rock, past a SLAB SECTION and then a small section of more featured rock to the top. There are many variations and they are all easy. So the difficulty will not identify it; the hardware will.

HOW TO GET TO IT FROM THE SADDLE, AND THE ONE THING TO KEEP STRAIGHT: from Red Pass the climbers' path winds WEST and up. Passing Red Mountain on your right and Red Pond on your left on the way in is the confirmation you are approaching the pass from the correct side.

A NAMING WARNING THAT COULD SEND YOU TO ANOTHER MOUNTAIN, AND IT IS A REAL ONE: the published location text for this route refers to a saddle between Lundin and East Lundin peaks, while the approach it gives goes to Red Pass and then west, which is Red Mountain's ground rather than Lundin's. TWO different published descriptions both called East Ridge exist on Red Mountain — one describing this saddle-to-summit line over two false summits, and one describing a ridge traverse from Point 5720 near the Kendall Katwalk, which its own author recommends nobody repeat. Three descriptions, one name. Fix the peak by the saddle and the three bolts, not by the route name.

IF YOU CONTINUE OVER THE FALSE SUMMITS toward the main peak, the sequence from the Red Mountain Saddle is: up the southeast side of the first false summit, a 30 ft class 3 gully down at its northwest end, right (north) to the big notch, 50 ft up slabs on the far side, a contour across the heathery northeast side of the second false summit, over that summit, then 100 ft of class 3 down a moderate gully to the final notch at about 5,840 ft below the main summit.

backups.detailed_rack: A single light rack to 2 inches plus a handful of slings is enough for the one short pitch; the rest is glacier and scrambling gear.
pro_tips: Combine with Eldorado's East Ridge, Klawatti Peak, and/or Austera Peak from the same high camp to make the most of the approach effort
watch_out: Moat width and difficulty change through the season — assess before committing to the crossing
backups.pro_needs: Minimal protection needed — one short low-5th pitch with a small rack.
backups.best_season: Best once the Inspiration Glacier moat below the tower opens enough to cross safely but before it becomes too wide late season; most parties combine it with an Eldorado/Klawatti/Austera traverse in July or August.
backups.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) up the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp near 7,600 ft where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. IMPORTANT — this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak itself, despite being filed under the same area: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.
backups.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb or rappel from a fixed rappel station directly below the top, landing back on the glacier for the return traverse to camp.
backups.bail: The route is short enough that retreat is simply reversing the line at any point; the main constraint is the glacier moat crossing, which can become harder to reverse as the day warms.

pitch_detail.notes: About 45 minutes north-northwest of the Eldorado East Ridge camp: climb high on the glacier to where it meets the rock and cross the moat onto the tower. Roped glacier travel; bring crampons, axe and pickets.
One short, low fifth-class pitch off the moat. A single rack to 2 in and slings for the anchor are enough.
Easy scrambling above the pitch to the top. Return by downclimbing, or rappel from the fixed station just below the summit back onto the glacier (bring a 60 m rope).

backups.itinerary: Day 1: approach to Eldorado high camp (~7,600 ft) via Eldorado Creek and Eldorado Glacier. Day 2: ~45 min glacier approach north/northwest to Tepeh Towers, climb the short route (~30 min), return to camp or continue on to Austera Peak. Day 3: hike out.

approach_variants.name: Forty-five minutes north-northwest off the Eldorado ice cap
approach_variants.notes: Everything below the ice cap is the standard Eldorado approach: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 at about 2,100 ft, backtrack a short way along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River (a large log or a braided ford, and it shifts year to year), then the steep unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,000-3,500 ft through old growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine meadows of Eldorado Creek basin — commonly five to six hours from the car. Push on to the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,600 ft. From that camp it is roughly a 45-minute roped glacier walk north-northwest to where the towers rise out of the icecap. The towers sit at the saddle you cross anyway to get from the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister — so most parties pass beneath them on the way to Klawatti, Austera or Dorado Needle and climb one as a side objective. Round trip from camp is well under two hours. Be clear about what this route is: TEPEH TOWERS IS NOT ON ELDORADO PEAK, despite being filed under the same area. It is a separate formation further along the icecap.
approach_variants.season: Once the Inspiration Glacier moat below the tower has opened enough to cross safely but before it becomes too wide late in the season — usually July or August, most often as part of an Eldorado/Klawatti/Austera traverse
hazards: Hidden crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier approach — roped travel and crevasse rescue gear, not an unroped stroll
The moat where the glacier rests against the rock, which is the whole gate on this climb
Loose rock near the summit
Softening snow bridges on the return, which is the real time constraint on such a short objective
approach_variants.baseFinding: TEPEH TOWERS IS AN ARÊTE OF MANY SPIRES, NOT ONE TOWER — that is the first thing to understand, and it is why the base finding here has to be about the moat rather than about the skyline. The formation is a rock arête poking out of the icecap northwest of the Inspiration Glacier, with Eldorado to the west and Klawatti to the northeast, and it carries a great many small spires. SO THE PROCEDURE IS: CLIMB HIGH ON THE GLACIER UNTIL THE ICE IS RESTING AGAINST THE ROCK, AND CROSS THE MOAT THERE. You are looking for the point where the snow meets the rock cleanly enough to step across; that point, not a particular spire seen from a distance, is what you navigate to. THE POSITIVE CONFIRMATION IS FIXED GEAR, AND IT IS THE ONLY DISCRIMINATOR PUBLISHED FOR THIS FORMATION: THE TOWER PARTIES CLIMB HAS RAPPEL ANCHORS DIRECTLY BELOW ITS SUMMIT. If you top out and there is no anchor below you, you have climbed a neighbouring spire — which is not dangerous here, but it is not the recorded line either. THE LENGTH TEST IS SHORT AND UNAMBIGUOUS: ONE short low-fifth pitch above the moat, then scrambling to the top. If you are running out a second and third rope length, you are on something else on the same arête. WHAT IS HONESTLY NOT KNOWN: no published account names which of the spires is the climbed one or gives a way to tell it from its neighbours at a distance. That gap is stated here rather than filled — treat the anchor below the summit as the confirmation and the moat as the navigation.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

backups.overview: Agnes Mountain is a dramatic, Matterhorn-shaped peak above Agnes Creek near the Stehekin/Suiattle divide, with a north face that drops 1,800 ft to Agnes Creek in only 1.5 miles. First climbed in 1936 by W. Ronald Frazier and Dan O'Brien via the West Fork of Agnes Creek, it remains rarely visited — historically only about one climbing party every 3-4 years, with just 14 recorded ascents by 1987 — due to its remote position and long approach.
backups.beta: This is the original first-ascent line established by Frazier and O'Brien in 1936. Modern mountaineers typically approach via the Agnes Creek Trail from Stehekin, establishing base camp in the upper basin (5,000-6,700 feet). The route involves Class 3-4 scrambling with some exposed sections and snow travel depending on season. The peak's north face rises steeply, creating objective hazards from rockfall. Technical rock climbing sections require helmets and rope skills.
backups.turnaround: Climbers should establish a turnaround time of mid-morning or early afternoon to allow sufficient daylight for descent through the technical sections and bushwhacking terrain. The route requires strong navigation skills and experience with alpine scrambling. Any delays on the summit pyramid necessitate descent before darkness falls.
backups.face: West side of the peak, above the West Fork Agnes Creek drainage
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: Cell service is unreliable or absent throughout the approach and on the mountain. Satellite communicator (Garmin inReach or similar) is essential for emergencies. The Stehekin area has limited communication infrastructure; emergency communication must be coordinated through Chelan County Sheriff's Office (911 or non-emergency dispatch 509-667-6851).
backups.descent: Descend via steep snow couloirs on the east or southeast side, then reverse the south ridge and the long Agnes Creek approach.

backups.detailed_rack: No exact cam/nut inventory is known. Terrain is a broad Class 2-4 ramp to a col, then a 30-ft chimney (5.5, with a harder ~5.8 alternate chimney used when the first proved impassable), then a final loose Class 4 scramble to the true summit. A light single rack of nuts plus cams roughly finger-to-hand size (~0.3-3in) covers the chimney/ledge terrain reasonably; a couple of doubled mid-size cams (1-2in) help for chimney stemming/stacking. This sizing is an estimate from the route's character, not a confirmed gear list.
pro_tips: Use the Stehekin shuttle to reach the Agnes Creek trailhead
Bring a rope and light rack — the summit block requires roped 5th-class climbing, not just scrambling
The summit register shows only about one party every 3-4 years, so expect no established boot track
watch_out: exposed 5.6-5.8 crux pitch on the summit block
log crossings of Agnes and Spruce Creek
backups.pro_needs: Both documented ascents describe the rock as loose/rotten in places ('test every single hold,' 'loose rock and hard dirt near the notch') rather than gear-placement-difficult — rockfall management is emphasized more than protection scarcity. The technical crux is a chimney (5.5, or 5.8 on the adjacent alternate line)
backups.approach: Start at the High Bridge Guard Station & Campground on Stehekin Valley Road (elev. ~1,600 ft) — reached from Stehekin by the NPS shuttle bus (about 11.3 miles) or on foot, since there is no through road; Stehekin itself is reached only by the Lady of the Lake/Lady Express ferry up Lake Chelan or by floatplane. From High Bridge, follow the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT southbound) up the valley through old-growth forest, a well-graded trail passing Three-Mile Camp and reaching Swamp Creek Camp at about mile 8.5 (roughly 5 hours for a loaded pack). Continue up-trail toward Mile 10, then leave the maintained tread to find a log crossing of Agnes Creek — the historic log is reportedly long gone, so scout for a currently-usable log or ford near Mile 10 — followed shortly by a second log crossing of Spruce Creek. From the far bank of Spruce Creek, the route turns into a steep, brushy, off-trail climb north/northwest up the hillside: plan on gaining the first ~1,000 vertical feet through thick slide alder, brush, and scrub trees, which is by far the slowest and most punishing part of the day. The brush eases noticeably above ~4,000 ft, and the cross-country line continues up open slabs and heather to "Upper Blue Basin," a rock-and-heather bench that serves as the standard high camp (figure on a very long day — roughly 10 hours from Swamp Creek Camp to camp in July). Water is reliable at Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek during the approach but is not guaranteed again until snowmelt/tarns near Upper Blue Basin, so top off before starting the brush climb. From high camp, the climb proper begins by crossing Icy–Spruce Pass and making a rising traverse over snow, talus, and rock slabs to reach the crest of Agnes' south ridge just south of Point 7760, where roped Class 4–5 rock leads up the ridge. Key hazards: creek crossings that vary year to year and may require route-finding to locate a safe log or ford, sustained steep brush with real potential to get off-route, and no maintained trail or cairns once you leave the Agnes Creek Trail. The standard line follows Asa Peak's northeast ridge onto Agnes' south ridge before the roped class 4-5 pitches begin.
backups.descent_text: This is not a walk-off. From the summit the party reverses the technical upper section, making three rappels down to reach the upper gully/notch below the crux 5.8 chimney and the roped 5.5–5.8 pitches climbed on the way up. Agnes Mountain is very seldom climbed (its summit register shows roughly one party every 3–4 years) and sits within North Cascades National Park backcountry, so there are no bolted or fixed chain anchors to expect — build natural anchors (slung horns, chockstones/gear) and plan to leave cord/webbing; a single 60m rope (or a doubled 30m) is enough for each rappel given the pitch lengths involved, but come prepared to construct your own anchors from scratch. Once back at the ~7,480-ft south col, there are two options: reverse the south ridge on the ascent line (Class 2–4 ledges and ramps), or, if snow conditions allow, drop down the east-facing snow couloir off the col — steeper but considerably faster, losing about 1,400 ft, protectable with snow pickets/flukes and running belays; this line demands firm, well-consolidated snow, an ice axe, and crampons, and is a poor choice if the gully has melted out to ice or scoured to rock. From the base of the couloir (or the bottom of the ridge line), make a long rising traverse south to a snow col near Point 7458 (~7,400 ft), then descend to the Upper Blue Basin high camp — the full summit-to-camp descent is a serious undertaking that can easily run 8+ hours, with the final stretch commonly finished by headlamp. From camp, reverse the approach: bushwhack back down through the brush below Spruce Creek, re-cross Spruce Creek and Agnes Creek on the same logs used on the way in, and hike back out the Agnes Creek Trail to High Bridge.
backups.bail: Retreat means reversing the lengthy approach.

itinerary.cal: Best mid-July through September once Agnes/Spruce Creek crossings drop and the summit snow couloir/rock is in reasonable condition; a North Cascades NP backcountry permit is required for camps along the Agnes Creek/PCT corridor, and Stehekin itself is only reached by boat, floatplane, or trail (no road) — build in ferry/shuttle timing.

access.fees: No NPS entrance fee; a free wilderness permit is required for overnight camping. The first ~2 miles from High Bridge (inside North Cascades NP) fall under the NPS backcountry-permit process; beyond that, in the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee NF), a free self-issue trailhead permit applies.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) inside Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft in wilderness.
access.permit: Free NPS backcountry permit (Wilderness Information Center/Golden West Visitor Center) only applies if camping within the first ~2 mi from High Bridge, inside North Cascades NP. For camps beyond that boundary — including the standard high camps used for this climb (Icy-Spruce Creek Pass, Upper Blue Basin, etc.) — a free, self-issue USFS wilderness permit obtained at the trailhead covers the Glacier Peak Wilderness portion; no NPS office visit is required for those.

Sisi Fire: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest closure order 06-17-02-2026-35 (Sisi Fire), in effect August 22 through December 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, closes the Pacific Crest Trail (Trail 2000) along Agnes Creek on the Chelan Ranger District, along with Agnes Creek Trail 1272, Agnes Gorge Trail 1281 and Swamp Creek Trail 1242. Off-trail route-finding in brushy, poorly-traveled terrain

Self-rescue awareness given the remote, boat-access-only approach

weather.typical: Drier east-side conditions, generally more stable than the west-side Cascades, but still subject to rapid mountain weather changes at elevation
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are possible during the July-August climbing window; early-season (June) and late-season (Sept-Oct) attempts carry elevated risk of new snow on the approach and summit block

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained, consequential exposure on the upper Class 3-4 scrambling terrain compounded by the loose rock; some parties describe a harder, more technical crux section near the summit, so parties should be prepared for more than casual scrambling. The remote, boat/floatplane-only Stehekin approach means any injury or fall carries a serious evacuation delay.

backups.rope_note: Steep snow couloir approach leads to a short roped 5.6 chimney crux pitch and a final 100 ft scramble to the summit; rope and light rack carried for the technical pitch.
backups.corrections: Trip-report beta describes a 5.6 chimney crux requiring rope/rock gear plus an ice-axe snow couloir approach — meaningfully harder than the 'Class 3-4' grade listed for this route.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three rappels reversing the technical upper section from the summit; build a natural anchor and expect to leave cord/webbing since there is no fixed hardware on this seldom-climbed route.
Second rappel continuing down toward the upper gully/notch below the crux 5.8 chimney; a single 60m rope (or doubled 30m) is adequate for each rappel given the pitch lengths involved.
Final rappel reaching the gully/notch below the crux chimney and the roped 5.5-5.8 pitches climbed on ascent; from here reverse the south ridge or, snow permitting, descend the east-facing couloir.

backups.rappel_count_note: Explicitly documented as three rappels down to the upper gully/notch below the crux 5.8 chimney; route is very seldom climbed with no bolted/fixed anchors, so natural anchors must be built and cord/webbing left behind.
rack: Single rope for the roped chimney pitch

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek trail, Spruce Creek and the brush climb to Upper Blue Basin
approach_variants.notes: There is no road into this valley: come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, then take the shuttle or walk to the guard station and campground at the road end. From there the Agnes Creek trail runs up the valley through old-growth forest on well-graded tread past a three-mile camp and on to the camp at Swamp Creek. Continue up-trail, then leave the maintained tread to find a log crossing of Agnes Creek — the historic log is long gone, so scout for a currently usable log or a ford — followed shortly by a second log crossing of Spruce Creek. From the far bank the route turns into a steep, brushy off-trail climb north and northwest up the hillside, and the first thousand vertical feet of slide alder, brush and scrub is by far the slowest part of the day.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends. Snow travel on the upper traverse varies with the season.
hazards: Creek crossings vary year to year and finding a safe log or ford is route-finding in itself
About a thousand vertical feet of sustained steep brush with real potential to get off-route
No maintained trail and no cairns once you leave the valley trail
The peak's north face rises steeply above the line and rockfall is an objective hazard
Water is reliable at the two creeks but not again until snowmelt and tarns near the high basin
The summit block carries genuine roped climbing — the crux chimney has been graded around 5.8, harder than a scramble grade suggests
The first chimney out of the snow gully dead-ends at an impassable horn and has had to be rappelled
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SECOND CHIMNEY, NOT THE FIRST, IS THE ROUTE — AND THAT IS THE WHOLE OF THE LAST 200 METRES. Above the high basin the climbing works onto the south ridge; a rubbly whaleback gives the first head-on view of the summit block, which is steep and forbidding from there and is the confirmation you are looking at the right thing. Drop to the south col around 7,480 ft, traverse a high snowpatch, and take the broad Class 2-3 ramp that runs closely to the left of a distinctive snow-filled gully. The ramp climbs straight, then dog-legs right to a short headwall; the ridge directly above that headwall is blocked by a large horn, so cross a small rib and drop about twenty-five feet to arrive at the top of the snow-filled gully you were paralleling. The exit from that gully is a chimney — and the obvious-looking first one dead-ends at another impassable horn. The correct chimney is the second, immediately to the right of the first. If you are in a chimney that closes out against a horn, you are in the wrong one: retreat and move right rather than forcing it.

climbing_route.label: Icy-Spruce Pass to the south ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: From high camp the climb proper begins by crossing Icy-Spruce Pass and making a rising traverse over snow, talus, and rock slabs to reach the crest of Agnes' south ridge just south of Point 7760. The standard line follows Asa Peak's northeast ridge onto Agnes' south ridge.

climbing_route.label: South ridge
climbing_route.notes: Roped Class 4-5 rock leads up the ridge; the roped class 4-5 pitches begin once the standard line gains Agnes' south ridge.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

bivy.name: West Fork Agnes Creek — the bivy under Agnes Mountain
bivy.notes: This is the working bivy zone for AGNES MOUNTAIN and it needs to be described honestly: THE TRAIL HAS ALL BUT VANISHED. What is marked on maps as the West Fork Agnes Creek trail is now a rough bushwhack up the drainage, last given any real maintenance a decade or more ago, and it leads nowhere except to the base of the mountain. Round trip from High Bridge is around seventeen miles of walking on top of the boat and the shuttle. The recommended line on the peak itself takes the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak first and then traverses to Agnes's south ridge, with short technical sections up to about 5.6 — so this is a climb rather than a scramble, on a peak that is seldom done precisely because the approach is so poor relative to its modest height. Navigation skill is not optional. Season is roughly July into September; earlier the creek is high and the brush is worse, later the days are too short for the mileage. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved ground and finding its own way up a drainage with no tread, this is the wrong objective.
bivy.water: The West Fork itself for as long as you are beside it, which is most of the way. Above it, snowmelt only and only early in the season. There is no reason to be short of water low down and every reason to carry it once you leave the creek.
bivy.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required for any overnight, and off-trail nights are handled as cross-country camping rather than as a named site — say what ground you intend to use when you arrange it rather than booking a camp that does not exist. Bear canisters are mandatory in cross-country ground where hanging is not possible, and free loaners come with the permit if you collect it in person. Camp on durable ground, gravel or rock rather than vegetation, and pack everything out.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. Whatever gravel bar, forest bench or open ground you reach, and small parties by necessity.

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

backups.name: South Ridge (via Asa Peak NE Ridge)
hazards: Significant rockfall/loose rock exposure on the ridge crest pitches.
Unbridged creek crossings (Agnes and Spruce Creek) on the approach, log crossings only.
Long enough summit day (reported ~19-20 hrs round trip) that headlamp travel on technical terrain should be expected.
backups.overview: The standard/recommended line on Agnes: gain the south ridge via a high traverse from Icy-Spruce Pass and the Northeast Ridge of Asa Peak, then climb a mix of 4th/low-5th-class ridge pitches and a 5.8 chimney crux on the summit headwall to the top.
backups.beta: Described as the recommended route: gain Asa Peak's Northeast Ridge, traverse to Agnes's south ridge, and climb short technical sections up to 5.6-5.8. From a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass, parties make a rising traverse over snow, talus, and slabs to the south ridge crest south of Point 7760, then rope up for several pitches of Class 4-5 rock on or left of the crest. Where the crest gets too craggy, downclimb one pitch to a ledge system and traverse to a whaleback with views of the summit block. From the 7,480-ft south col, traverse a high snowpatch and ascend a broad Class 2-3 ramp just left of a snow-filled gully, dog-legging right to a headwall; a 5.8 chimney (the crux) and one more roped pitch lead to a final ~100-ft Class 2-3 scramble to the summit.
backups.turnaround: One documented ascent took 10.6 hours from high camp to the summit and 8.8 hours to descend (including headlamp travel), for a ~19-20 hour round trip — build in a very conservative alpine start and be willing to turn around well before dusk given the rappelling required on descent.
backups.rappels: 3 rappels through the headwall/chimney band to reach the upper gully, then an ~1,400-ft descending traverse of an east-facing snow couloir back to the south col
backups.face: South Ridge, reached via the Northeast Ridge of neighboring Asa Peak; upper headwall faces roughly NW
backups.descent: Downclimb the final scramble, then reverse the roped pitches/chimney with 3 rappels to the upper gully, and descend the ~1,400-ft east-facing snow couloir (flukes/running belays) back to the south col before reversing the ridge traverse to camp.
obj_haz: A deep, exposed bergschrund/moat blocking direct glacier access near the ridge
Loose rock and significant exposure on the ridge crest
Steep snow couloir on descent (avalanche/glissade hazard)
Long, brushy multi-day approach with unbridged creek crossings

timing.recommendedStart: Very early (roughly 6 AM) from high camp, based on a documented 10.6-hour push arriving at the summit at 4:30 PM

backups.detailed_rack: A light rock rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the low-5th-class ridge pitches and the 5.8 chimney, plus a rope, rappel device, and gear for a snow couloir descent (axe, and ideally pickets/flukes for the descent).
what_to_bring: Multi-day backpacking/camping gear for a 4-5 day trip
Approach shoes plus climbing shoes/boots suited to 5.8
Headlamp (long summit days reported into the night)
pro_tips: Camp at Icy-Spruce Pass rather than lower down to shorten the very long summit day.
The whaleback ledge system partway up the ridge gives the first real view of the summit block and headwall — use it to route-find the dog-leg to the chimney.
watch_out: A deep, scary moat/bergschrund blocks any attempt to escape onto the neighboring glacier.
The descent couloir is steep snow requiring flukes/running belays — do not underestimate it relative to the rock climbing.
backups.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack sufficient for sustained 4th/low-5th class with a short 5.8 crux; snow protection (flukes/pickets) needed for the descent couloir rather than the ascent itself.
backups.best_season: July through September; snow can still cover the col and gully in early July, which is useful for the couloir descent but adds route-finding difficulty on the ridge.
backups.approach: From High Bridge in Stehekin, follow the PCT/Agnes Creek Trail south roughly 8-10 miles (about 5.2 hours to a Swamp Creek-area camp) to the Agnes Creek/Spruce Creek confluence. Cross Agnes Creek on a log, then Spruce Creek on another log shortly after, and climb steeply northwest off-trail through brush, talus, and slabs to a camp near Upper Blue Basin (~5,000 ft), then continue to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass (~6,760 ft) for the summit push.
backups.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb the last ~100 ft of Class 2-3 terrain, then reverse the roped pitch above the chimney and rappel the 5.8 chimney/headwall (3 rappels total) to regain the upper gully. From there, descend an east-facing snow couloir for roughly 1,400 vertical feet using snow flukes and running belays back to the south col at ~7,480 ft, then reverse the traverse and ridge pitches back toward Icy-Spruce Pass camp — a round trip reported at roughly 19-20 hours from high camp on one ascent.
backups.bail: Retreat down the south ridge is via the same 3 rappels through the chimney/headwall band into the upper gully, then the snow couloir back to the south col; avoid attempting to escape onto the adjacent glacier due to a large bergschrund/moat.

pitch_detail.notes: South ridge crest, several pitches, climbing on or left of the crest; rope up starting south of Point 7760.
Where the crest becomes too craggy, downclimb one pitch to a ledge system and traverse north to a whaleback formation.
From the 7,480-ft south col, traverse a high snowpatch then ascend a broad ramp just left of a snow-filled gully, dog-legging right to the headwall.
Crux chimney on the summit headwall.
One additional roped pitch above the chimney.
Final ~100 ft of scrambling to the true summit.

backups.itinerary: Day 1: High Bridge to a Swamp Creek-area camp (~8.5 mi PCT). Day 2: cross Agnes and Spruce Creeks, climb to Upper Blue Basin camp (~5,000 ft). Day 3: move to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass (~6,760 ft). Day 4: summit push via the south ridge and chimney crux (reported ~10.6 hr up, ~8.8 hr down); return to high camp. Day 5: hike out to High Bridge.

climbing_route.label: Traverse to the south col (~7,480 ft)
climbing_route.notes: The classic published line gains the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak and traverses onto Agnes' south ridge. From an Icy-Spruce Pass high camp the travelled variation goes over Point 7458, drops to a notch near 7,200 ft, crosses a snowfield at the head of Yew Creek, then climbs a steep, narrow snow couloir on the south side of Agnes for roughly 1,300 ft to the south col at about 7,480 ft. Carry axe and crampons: this couloir has been found firm and steep, and it is the descent line as well. Late in the season expect a moat where the snow pulls away from the rock at the top.

climbing_route.label: Lower south ridge
climbing_route.notes: Rope up. Several short pitches on or just left of the ridge crest, on rock that is broken and demands testing. Where the crest steepens past reason, the usual solution is to lose about a pitch to a ledge system on the west side and traverse north beneath the difficulties to a rubbly whaleback — the first place the summit block comes into view. Route-finding here is the real difficulty; committing to the crest can leave a party downclimbing loose ground under load.

climbing_route.label: Summit block ramp
climbing_route.notes: From the col the way onto the summit block is a broad ramp immediately left of a distinctive snow-filled gully. Follow it up and dog-leg right toward the headwall. Do not try to stay on the crest above: it is blocked by a large horn. Rockfall generated by a party above is the main hazard on the ramp.

climbing_route.label: Crux chimney
climbing_route.notes: Two chimneys break the headwall out of the snow gully. The left-hand, more obvious one has been found impassable; the second, immediately right, is the one that goes and is the hardest climbing on the peak. Its grade is reported anywhere from 5.6 to 5.8 depending on party and conditions — treat 5.8 as the planning figure. Rock quality is poor: holds have been reported moving under hand, so test everything and belay from out of the fall line. Snow or ice in the back of the chimney early in the season adds significantly to the difficulty.

climbing_route.label: Upper wall and summit
climbing_route.notes: One further roped pitch above the chimney, then roughly 100 ft of exposed scrambling on the west side of the block to the top. Loose rock and real exposure — most parties stay roped. Descent is by two or three rappels back down the summit block, then the south couloir on running belays for about 1,400 ft; the moat at the top of that couloir and the loose ground beside it are where parties knock rock onto each other, so descend one at a time or well spaced. Agnes is climbed only every few years, so anchors and any fixed gear should be treated as unknown and replaced.
